changes.new: ### Adversarial regularization of text embeddings A token identifier cannot be changed by an infinitesimal amount. An embedding vector can. For a sequence of token vectors, concatenate the non-padding coordinates into $s$. A text classifier can then be trained on $s+r$, even though this perturbed vector usually has no corresponding sentence. [Miyato, Dai and Goodfellow, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/html/1605.07725v4#S2) use this construction to regularize an LSTM classifier. Their threat model does not establish resistance to word substitutions or malicious user text: the regularizer operates inside the model. For a human label $y$, write the cross-entropy as $\ell(s,y;\theta)=-\log p_\theta(y\mid s)$. Its linear approximation is $$ \ell(s+r,y;\hat\theta) \approx \ell(s,y;\hat\theta)+g^\top r, \qquad g=\nabla_s\ell(s,y;\hat\theta). $$ Cauchy–Schwarz gives $g^\top r\le\varepsilon\|g\|_2$ inside an $\ell_2$ ball. For nonzero $g$, the maximum of this approximation is therefore attained at $$ r_{\mathrm{adv}}=\varepsilon\frac{g}{\|g\|_2}. $$ The sign is positive because $g$ differentiates the **loss**. If $g$ instead differentiates $\log p_\theta(y\mid s)$, its sign must be negated. Using a negative cross-entropy gradient would make a loss-reducing step. With $g=(3,4)$ and $\varepsilon=0.1$, the maximizing step is $(0.06,0.08)$ and the linearized loss increase is $0.5$. Reversing the step gives $-0.5$. The outer update minimizes the clean loss plus the loss at the selected perturbation. The current weights are held fixed while constructing $r$; the outer gradient treats $r$ as a constant. Embedding and classifier parameters still receive gradients through the recomputed perturbed prediction. Detaching the perturbation is different from detaching the embedding table for the whole update. #### The radius depends on embedding scale Multiplying every embedding by a large constant and compensating in the next layer can leave clean predictions unchanged while making a fixed additive radius relatively smaller. The original text method controls this degree of freedom with frequency-weighted coordinate normalization. For vocabulary vectors $v_j$ and frequencies $f_j$ summing to one, $$ \begin{aligned} \mu_k&=\sum_j f_jv_{jk},\\ \sigma_k^2&=\sum_j f_j(v_{jk}-\mu_k)^2,\\ \bar v_{jk}&=\frac{v_{jk}-\mu_k}{\sqrt{\sigma_k^2+\delta}}. \end{aligned} $$ This is not unit-length normalization of each token and is not minibatch LayerNorm. The statistics are computed over vocabulary entries with corpus frequency weights. The released [embedding layer](https://github.com/tensorflow/models/blob/feec308b23edb6a3c5745a2d11890db3601cc0b5/research/adversarial_text/layers.py) uses $\delta=10^{-6}$. For vocabulary vectors $(1,0)$, $(3,4)$ and $(0,1)$ with frequencies $(0.5,0.25,0.25)$, the mean is $(1.25,1.25)$ and the coordinate variances are $(1.1875,2.6875)$. The classifier below looks up the first two vectors, while all three contribute to the normalization statistics. The next program checks these moments, selects an adversarial direction and differentiates the outer loss. It uses a two-token linear classifier, not the paper's LSTM or a robustness benchmark. ```python import torch import torch.nn.functional as F dtype = torch.float64 v = torch.tensor([[1., 0.], [3., 4.], [0., 1.]], dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True) frequency = torch.tensor([.5, .25, .25], dtype=dtype) w = torch.tensor([1., 0., 0., 1.], dtype=dtype, requires_grad=True) def embeddings(): mean = (frequency[:, None] * v).sum(0) variance = (frequency[:, None] * (v - mean).square()).sum(0) return (v - mean) / (variance + 1e-6).sqrt(), mean, variance normalized, mean, variance = embeddings() torch.testing.assert_close(mean, torch.tensor([1.25, 1.25], dtype=dtype)) torch.testing.assert_close(variance, torch.tensor([1.1875, 2.6875], dtype=dtype)) s = normalized[:2].reshape(-1) logits = torch.stack([s.new_zeros(()), w @ s])[None] clean = F.cross_entropy(logits, torch.tensor([0])) g, = torch.autograd.grad(clean, s) radius = .2 r = (radius * g / g.norm()).detach() assert not r.requires_grad torch.testing.assert_close(r.norm(), r.new_tensor(radius)) plus = F.cross_entropy( torch.stack([s.new_zeros(()), w.detach() @ (s.detach() + r)])[None], torch.tensor([0])) minus = F.cross_entropy( torch.stack([s.new_zeros(()), w.detach() @ (s.detach() - r)])[None], torch.tensor([0])) assert plus > clean.detach() > minus # Recompute the outer graph; r remains fixed but v and w are trainable. new_s = embeddings()[0][:2].reshape(-1) outer = F.cross_entropy( torch.stack([new_s.new_zeros(()), w @ new_s])[None], torch.tensor([0])) outer += F.cross_entropy( torch.stack([new_s.new_zeros(()), w @ (new_s + r)])[None], torch.tensor([0])) outer.backward() assert torch.isfinite(v.grad).all() and v.grad.norm() > 0 assert torch.isfinite(w.grad).all() and w.grad.norm() > 0 print("clean / increased / decreased", clean.item(), plus.item(), minus.item()) print("embedding gradient norm", v.grad.norm().item()) ``` A radius for the concatenated sequence is also different from the same radius independently assigned to every token: with $T$ equally perturbed tokens, the latter has total norm $\sqrt{T}\varepsilon$. Padding should not consume the perturbation budget. The released text VAT code masks padding and the final EOS position before normalizing its search vector; it measures the norm across the sequence and embedding dimensions. These choices belong to the algorithm specification, not just its tensor implementation. FreeLB does not require this original vocabulary normalization, so its radius cannot be transferred numerically without accounting for its embedding scale and norm convention. #### Reading the original text-classification experiment The IMDb experiment in [Miyato et al., §§4.2–5.1, Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/1605.07725v4#S5.T2) starts from a language-model-pretrained, unidirectional LSTM with embedding dropout. The following entries are reported test-error percentages: | Training configuration | IMDb test error, % | | --- | ---: | | Baseline without embedding normalization | 7.33 | | Normalized baseline | 7.39 | | Random perturbations on labelled examples | 7.20 | | Random perturbations on labelled and unlabelled examples | 6.78 | | Labelled adversarial training | 6.21 | | VAT | 5.91 | | Adversarial training plus VAT | 6.09 | The normalized baseline alone is not better than the unnormalized one. VAT has access to unlabelled inputs, so 6.21 versus 5.91 compares both the target construction and the available training inputs. Combining the two penalties is not best in this table. The authors tune both embedding dropout and the perturbation radius on validation data; the numbers are not consequences of choosing one universal radius. Table 3 also illustrates how the downstream objective changes the embedding geometry. “Bad” is the third neighbour of “good” in the baseline, but the nineteenth after adversarial training and the twenty-first after VAT. Opposite-sentiment adjectives can occur in similar grammatical contexts; sentiment supervision gives the classifier a reason to distinguish them. This is one model's neighbour analysis, not a guarantee that all antonyms separate or that cosine proximity measures meaning independently of the training task. When labels are unavailable, a clean prediction can supply a distribution target instead. The full derivation of [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/11 Pre-training и Scaling/41e Обучение с частичной разметкой — pseudo-labeling и FixMatch#virtual-adversarial-training|VAT, its Hessian direction and finite-difference search]] is kept in the semi-supervised chapter. #### FreeLB: gradients from every ascent point In ordinary multi-step adversarial training, the inner search locates a high-loss point and the outer step uses the loss at that final point. [FreeLB, §3 and Algorithm 1](https://arxiv.org/html/1909.11764v2#S3) retains the parameter gradient at each visited point. The weights remain fixed during the $K$ inner passes: $$ \begin{aligned} g_\theta&=\frac1K\sum_{t=0}^{K-1} \nabla_\theta\ell(f_\theta(s+\delta_t),y),\\ h_t&=\nabla_\delta\ell(f_\theta(s+\delta_t),y),\\ \delta_{t+1} &=\Pi_{\|\delta\|_F\le\varepsilon} \left(\delta_t+\alpha\frac{h_t}{\|h_t\|_F}\right),\\ \theta_{\mathrm{new}}&=\theta-\eta g_\theta. \end{aligned} $$ The last perturbation update need not be computed if its result will not be used. The parameter update still occurs only once. Stopping gradients through the sequence of perturbations avoids differentiating the search trajectory; it does not discard the parameter gradients computed along it. Consider the scalar loss $\ell(\theta,\delta)= \frac12[\theta(0.2+\delta)-1]^2$, with $\theta=0.8$, $\delta_0=0$, radius $0.3$, ascent step $0.15$ and $K=3$. This constructed example uses zero initialization to make every intermediate value visible; the original algorithm uses random initialization. | Ascent point | $\delta_t$ | Residual | Parameter gradient | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | 0 | $0$ | $-0.84$ | $-0.168$ | | 1 | $-0.15$ | $-0.96$ | $-0.048$ | | 2 | $-0.30$ | $-1.08$ | $0.108$ | The average parameter gradient is $-0.036$, while the final-point gradient is $0.108$. Their signs differ. With learning rate $0.1$, the accumulated update gives $0.8036$; an update using only the last point gives $0.7892$. ```python import torch theta = torch.tensor(.8, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True) delta = torch.tensor(0., dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True) gradients, points = [], [] for step in range(3): loss = .5 * (theta * (.2 + delta) - 1.).square() gt, gd = torch.autograd.grad(loss, (theta, delta)) points.append(delta.detach().item()) gradients.append(gt.detach()) if step < 2: delta = (delta.detach() + .15 * gd.detach().sign()).clamp(-.3, .3) delta.requires_grad_() average = torch.stack(gradients).mean() torch.testing.assert_close(torch.tensor(points), torch.tensor([0., -.15, -.3])) torch.testing.assert_close(average, average.new_tensor(-.036)) accumulated_update = theta.detach() - .1 * average last_point_update = theta.detach() - .1 * gradients[-1] torch.testing.assert_close(accumulated_update, average.new_tensor(.8036)) torch.testing.assert_close(last_point_update, average.new_tensor(.7892)) print("parameter gradients", [g.item() for g in gradients]) print("updates", accumulated_update.item(), last_point_update.item()) ``` “Free” refers to retaining parameter gradients during backward passes already used to search for perturbations. The method still performs $K$ forward/backward passes; it is not a one-pass clean update at zero extra cost. A larger virtual batch of perturbed views is not a larger set of independent labelled sentences. Dropout changes the function being maximized. FreeLB's §3.3 keeps the same sampled dropout masks across the inner ascent points for one minibatch; fresh masks are sampled for later minibatches. Resampling at every ascent point would make each step optimize a different sampled network. This is distinct from [R-Drop](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.14448v2)'s comparison of two independently sampled dropout predictions: R-Drop does not select a worst-case embedding perturbation. #### SMART: local smoothness and a moving reference ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/consistency-training-2026-10-29/smart-boundaries.png|Original SMART decision boundaries, both panels and complete caption]] *Haoming Jiang and co-authors, [SMART, ACL 2020, Figure 1](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.197.pdf#page=4), [CC BY 4.0](https://aclanthology.org/faq/copyright/). Complete original figure and caption rendered from the vector PDF at 400 dpi. Both panels are retained. The dotted line in panel (b) is the earlier boundary from (a); the squares depict local neighbourhoods. This is a schematic illustration, not a measured robustness result.* [SMART, §3](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.197/) combines two penalties. Its local penalty compares predictions at a clean embedding and a nearby high-disagreement embedding. For classification it uses the sum of the two KL directions. Write $P_i=p_\theta(\cdot\mid s_i)$ and $Q_i(r)=p_\theta(\cdot\mid s_i+r)$: $$ \begin{aligned} J(P,Q)&=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\\ &\quad+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P),\\ \mathcal R_s(\theta)&=\frac1n\sum_i \max_{\|r_i\|_p\le\varepsilon}J(P_i,Q_i(r_i)). \end{aligned} $$ The human-labelled task loss remains part of $\mathcal F(\theta)=\mathcal L(\theta)+\lambda_s\mathcal R_s(\theta)$. The inner maximization is approximated with projected ascent. The classification divergence is not the squared error used for regression, and it is not the single-direction detached-target VAT objective. SMART also discourages an outer update from changing clean predictions too far from a reference model. With $\tilde P_{t,i}=p_{\tilde\theta_t}(\cdot\mid s_i)$, its subproblem is $$ \begin{aligned} D_{\mathrm{Breg}}(\theta,\tilde\theta_t) &=\frac1n\sum_i J(P_i,\tilde P_{t,i}),\\ \theta_{t+1} &\approx\arg\min_\theta \left[\mathcal F(\theta)+\mu D_{\mathrm{Breg}}(\theta,\tilde\theta_t)\right]. \end{aligned} $$ The vanilla version uses the previous parameters as reference. The momentum version maintains $\tilde\theta_{t+1}=(1-\beta)\theta_{t+1}+\beta\tilde\theta_t$. The reference is fixed during a subproblem; a small number of Adam steps approximates its solution. An EMA of parameters is not generally the same as an average of predicted probabilities. The penalty measures changed predictions on the sampled inputs, rather than Euclidean distance between parameter arrays. A one-input example isolates this effect. Suppose the reference assigns probability $0.2$ to class 1, while the current human label is class 1. Minimizing only $-\log p$ pushes $p$ toward 1. Adding $\mu J((1-p,p),(0.8,0.2))$ gives an interior compromise. The following grid calculation evaluates the actual symmetric divergence; it omits the separate local perturbation penalty and is not an implementation of the full SMART optimizer. ```python import torch p = torch.linspace(.0001, .9999, 10001, dtype=torch.float64) current = torch.stack([1 - p, p], dim=1) reference = torch.tensor([.8, .2], dtype=torch.float64) symmetric_kl = ( current * (current.log() - reference.log()) + reference * (reference.log() - current.log()) ).sum(dim=1) best = [] for mu in (0., 1., 5.): objective = -p.log() + mu * symmetric_kl optimum = p[objective.argmin()].item() best.append(optimum) print("mu", mu, "best probability of the human target", optimum) assert best[0] > best[1] > best[2] > .2 ``` Neither penalty guarantees preservation of every capability learned during pretraining. The reference constraint is evaluated on available inputs, and the local constraint concerns a chosen embedding norm. A claim about real text attacks, retained tasks or generalization still requires a separate evaluation protocol. ### Что даёт сертификат

changes.new: ## VAT: consistency in the most sensitive local direction For an unlabelled input, there is no human target with which to compute an adversarial cross-entropy gradient. Virtual adversarial training uses the model's current distribution as a fixed target: $q=p_{\hat\theta}(\cdot\mid s)$. Define $$ \begin{aligned} D(r)&=D_{\mathrm{KL}} \bigl(q\|p_{\hat\theta}(\cdot\mid s+r)\bigr),\\ r_{\mathrm{vadv}}&\approx \arg\max_{\|r\|_2\le\varepsilon} D(r),\\ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{VAT}}(\theta)&= D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(q\|p_\theta(\cdot\mid s+r_{\mathrm{vadv}})\bigr). \end{aligned} $$ Both $q$ and the selected $r_{\mathrm{vadv}}$ are treated as constants when differentiating the outer loss with respect to $\theta$. The labelled loss still anchors class identities. The consistency regularizer can be averaged over labelled and unlabelled inputs. Agreement with an incorrect clean prediction does not establish that either answer is correct. This construction and the approximation below follow [Miyato et al., VAT, §III](https://arxiv.org/html/1704.03976v2#S3); the embedding-space application is specified in [Miyato, Dai and Goodfellow, §§2–3](https://arxiv.org/html/1605.07725v4#S2). ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/consistency-training-2026-10-29/vat.gif|Original author animation of VAT predictions and local distributional smoothness]] *Takeru Miyato, original `vat.gif` from [vat_tf, revision c5125d2](https://github.com/takerum/vat_tf/blob/c5125d267531ce0f10b2238cf95604d287de63c8/vat.gif), MIT; [license copy](/licenses/vat-tf-c5125d2-MIT.txt). The complete 14-frame, 320×180 animation is unchanged and is not upscaled. The left panel shows predictions and the right panel LDS, the local distributional-smoothness penalty; blue marks larger local changes than grey. The coloured diamonds supply labelled anchors; the surrounding points also affect consistency without receiving human labels. This synthetic two-dimensional illustration does not measure the accuracy of a text classifier.* ### Why the gradient at the clean input cannot select a direction At $r=0$, the two distributions agree, so $D(0)=0$. KL is nonnegative. For a differentiable model, zero is therefore a local minimum and $\nabla_rD(0)=0$. An ordinary normalized first-gradient step has no direction to normalize. The local quadratic approximation instead uses the Hessian: $$ D(r)\approx\frac12r^\top Hr,\qquad H=\left.\nabla_r^2D(r)\right|_{r=0}. $$ Within an $\ell_2$ ball, this quadratic is largest along a dominant eigenvector of the positive-semidefinite $H$. Constructing a full $TD\times TD$ matrix for $T$ token vectors of dimension $D$ is unnecessary. For a unit vector $d$ and a small positive $\xi$, $$ Hd\approx\frac{\nabla_rD(\xi d)-\nabla_rD(0)}{\xi} =\frac{\nabla_rD(\xi d)}{\xi}. $$ After normalization, the positive factor $1/\xi$ cancels. Start from a random unit $d$, compute the gradient at $r=\xi d$, normalize it, and repeat for the chosen power-iteration budget. The final perturbation has magnitude $\varepsilon$. One iteration is an approximation, not an exact solution of the nonlinear inner maximization. A zero Hessian, a degenerate leading eigenspace or an uninformative initial direction needs explicit handling. A binary classifier makes the calculation visible. Let $p(1\mid s)=\sigma(w^\top s)$, with $w=(2,1)$ and $s=(0,0)$. The clean target is $(1/2,1/2)$, and $$ H=\frac14ww^\top= \begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1/4\end{pmatrix}. $$ Its eigenvalues are $0$ and $1.25$. A unit direction parallel to $(2,1)$ changes the logit; the perpendicular direction $(1,-2)/\sqrt5$ does not. For $\varepsilon=0.2$, the first direction produces logit $0.2\sqrt5$ and divergence $\log\cosh(0.1\sqrt5)$. The perpendicular perturbation gives zero divergence in this linear model. A random direction need not expose the largest change even when its norm is identical. ```python import math import torch w = torch.tensor([2., 1.], dtype=torch.float64) q = torch.tensor([.5, .5], dtype=torch.float64) def divergence(r): logits = torch.stack([r.new_zeros(()), w @ r]) return (q * (q.log() - logits.log_softmax(0))).sum() zero = torch.zeros(2, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True) gradient, = torch.autograd.grad(divergence(zero), zero) torch.testing.assert_close(gradient, torch.zeros_like(gradient), atol=1e-14, rtol=0) hessian = torch.autograd.functional.hessian(divergence, zero) torch.testing.assert_close(hessian, .25 * torch.outer(w, w)) eigenvalues = torch.linalg.eigvalsh(hessian) torch.testing.assert_close(eigenvalues, torch.tensor([0., 1.25], dtype=w.dtype)) d = torch.tensor([1., -1.], dtype=w.dtype) d /= d.norm() probe = (.001 * d).requires_grad_() g, = torch.autograd.grad(divergence(probe), probe) direction = (g / g.norm()).detach() torch.testing.assert_close(direction.abs(), (w / w.norm()).abs()) radius = .2 sensitive = radius * direction perpendicular = radius * torch.tensor([1., -2.], dtype=w.dtype) / math.sqrt(5) expected = math.log(math.cosh(.1 * math.sqrt(5))) assert abs(divergence(sensitive).item() - expected) < 1e-12 assert abs(divergence(perpendicular).item()) < 1e-14 print("Hessian", hessian.tolist(), "eigenvalues", eigenvalues.tolist()) print("sensitive / perpendicular KL", divergence(sensitive).item(), divergence(perpendicular).item()) ``` The sign of a quadratic eigenvector is arbitrary; finite-radius nonlinear losses need not be symmetric. Increasing the number of power iterations improves a direction estimate under the local spectral assumptions, but does not certify a global adversary for an arbitrary neural network. The probe radius $\xi$, perturbation radius $\varepsilon$, regularizer weight and number of iterations have different roles. An experiment that fixes some of them has not eliminated them from the algorithm. ### A complete embedding-space VAT update For text, the continuous variable $s$ is obtained after embedding lookup. The normalization and sign convention of labelled adversarial training are developed in [[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/19 Deployment, Reliability и MLOps/05 Устойчивость ML-систем#embedding-adversarial-training|embedding-space adversarial regularization]]. The original text implementation masks both padding and EOS while constructing its perturbation. A budget over all coordinates of one sequence is different from an independent budget for every token. The following small classifier uses masked mean pooling and has no EOS, dropout or batch normalization. Its perturbations exclude padding and have one $\ell_2$ budget per sequence. Vocabulary-frequency normalization is omitted in this fixture. These choices isolate gradient flow; they do not reproduce the paper's LSTM training protocol. ```python import torch import torch.nn.functional as F torch.manual_seed(19) dtype = torch.float64 embedding = torch.nn.Embedding(6, 2, padding_idx=0).to(dtype) head = torch.nn.Linear(2, 2).to(dtype) parameters = list(embedding.parameters()) + list(head.parameters()) optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(parameters, lr=.1) unlabelled = torch.tensor([[1, 2, 0], [3, 0, 0], [4, 5, 0]]) labelled = torch.tensor([[1, 2, 0], [3, 4, 0]]) human_targets = torch.tensor([0, 1]) mask = (unlabelled != 0)[..., None] def classify(vectors, valid): count = valid.sum(dim=1) assert (count > 0).all() return head((vectors * valid).sum(dim=1) / count) def unit(vector): vector = vector * mask norm = vector.flatten(1).norm(dim=1)[:, None, None] return vector / norm.clamp_min(1e-12) def kl(target, logits): return (target * (target.log() - logits.log_softmax(dim=-1))).sum(-1).mean() optimizer.zero_grad() search_vectors = embedding(unlabelled).detach() q = classify(search_vectors, mask).softmax(-1).detach() probe = (.001 * unit(torch.randn_like(search_vectors))).detach().requires_grad_() search_loss = kl(q, classify(search_vectors + probe, mask)) g, = torch.autograd.grad(search_loss, probe) r = (.3 * unit(g)).detach() assert all(p.grad is None for p in parameters) assert torch.equal(r[~mask.expand_as(r)], torch.zeros_like(r[~mask.expand_as(r)])) torch.testing.assert_close(r.flatten(1).norm(dim=1), r.new_full((3,), .3)) # Only this outer graph updates the embedding table and classifier. clean_labelled = classify(embedding(labelled), (labelled != 0)[..., None]) supervised = F.cross_entropy(clean_labelled, human_targets) vat = kl(q, classify(embedding(unlabelled) + r, mask)) loss = supervised + vat before = [p.detach().clone() for p in parameters] loss.backward() assert not q.requires_grad and not r.requires_grad assert all(p.grad is not None and torch.isfinite(p.grad).all() for p in parameters) assert embedding.weight.grad[0].count_nonzero() == 0 optimizer.step() assert any(not torch.equal(a, b) for a, b in zip(before, parameters)) print("supervised / VAT", supervised.item(), vat.item()) print("perturbation norms", r.flatten(1).norm(dim=1).tolist()) ``` The inner derivative is taken only with respect to the probe; it does not accumulate an optimizer gradient in the parameter arrays. The outer pass recomputes embeddings, so the shared table remains trainable. The clean distribution and selected perturbation are held fixed for this outer derivative. The original [VAT implementation](https://github.com/takerum/vat_tf/blob/c5125d267531ce0f10b2238cf95604d287de63c8/vat.py) uses the same stop-gradient separation. For $K$ search iterations, the VAT paper counts $K$ search backpropagations, one regularizer backpropagation and one supervised backpropagation. Shared or batched execution can change actual runtime. With independent dropout samples or changing batch-normalization state, two predictions at the same unperturbed input may already differ; a search must specify how that stochastic state is controlled. A small loss at the selected perturbation is not a certificate against all embedding perturbations, much less against arbitrary changes of text. ## UDA: consistency across augmented text Embedding perturbations need not produce readable text. UDA instead constructs another input, such as a back-translated sentence, and trains the prediction on that input to match a fixed distribution from the original. The label-preserving assumption is about the augmentation: changing “the treatment did not help” to “the treatment helped” would supply a wrong consistency target even if both strings are fluent. ![[02 Areas/ML & DL/00 Учебник/Assets/Figures/curated/consistency-training-2026-10-29/uda-fixmatch.png|Original UDA and FixMatch text-training comparison with complete caption]] *Po-Wei Huang and co-authors, [Lightweight Contextual Logical Structure Recovery, Figure 2](https://aclanthology.org/2022.sdp-1.5.pdf#page=5), [CC BY 4.0](https://aclanthology.org/faq/copyright/). Complete original figure and caption rendered at 400 dpi. This is the authors' text-domain adaptation: EDA on the right is their weak text augmentation, not part of FixMatch's original image protocol. Within each method the repeated backbone boxes share parameters. The left branch compares distributions; the right creates hard pseudo-labels. Gradient stops, confidence gates and the KL direction are specified by the equations and original code below, not by the arrows alone.* The original UDA [method, §§2 and A](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12848v6#S2) adds a consistency term to supervised cross-entropy. For $M$ unlabelled inputs, obtain clean probabilities $q_i$, augmented predictions $p_i$ and, optionally, sharpened clean targets: $$ \begin{aligned} q_i&=p_{\hat\theta}(\cdot\mid u_i),\\ \tilde q_{ic} &=\frac{\exp(z_{ic}/T)} {\sum_j\exp(z_{ij}/T)},\\ m_i&=\mathbf1[\max_c q_{ic}>\beta],\\ p_i&=p_\theta(\cdot\mid A(u_i)),\\ \mathcal L_u&=\frac1M\sum_i m_i D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\tilde q_i\|p_i). \end{aligned} $$ The target $\tilde q_i$ and gate $m_i$ are held fixed in the outer derivative; the augmented prediction $p_i$ supplies the parameter gradient. Here $z_i$ contains the clean logits, $T$ is the target-distribution temperature and $\beta$ the confidence threshold. The gate uses **unsharpened** probabilities. Otherwise, sharpening could make an uncertain prediction pass the same gate that was meant to reject it. The original text [implementation](https://github.com/google-research/uda/blob/960684e363251772a5938451d4d2bc0f1da9e24b/text/uda.py) uses strict `>` for this confidence test and divides by the entire unlabelled batch, including rejected examples. The paper writes cross-entropy for the soft-target objective; the released text implementation computes KL. With the target detached, $\mathrm{CE}(\tilde q,p)=H(\tilde q)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\tilde q\|p)$. The two losses have the same gradient with respect to the prediction logits, but different numeric values. Neither is identical to replacing $\tilde q$ by its most likely class. For clean predictions $(0.9,0.1)$, $(0.8,0.2)$ and $(0.6,0.4)$, let $\beta=0.8$ and $T=0.5$. Only the first example passes. Squaring and renormalizing its probabilities gives $(81/82,1/82)$. If the augmented prediction is $(0.6,0.4)$, its logit gradient is $\bigl((0.6,0.4)-(81/82,1/82)\bigr)/3$. The other two examples have zero masked gradients. ```python import torch import torch.nn.functional as F clean_logits = torch.tensor([[.9, .1], [.8, .2], [.6, .4]], dtype=torch.float64).log().requires_grad_() aug_logits = torch.tensor([[.6, .4], [.3, .7], [.2, .8]], dtype=torch.float64).log().requires_grad_() q = clean_logits.detach().softmax(-1) target = (clean_logits.detach() / .5).softmax(-1) mask = q.max(-1).values > .8 per_example = (target * (target.log() - aug_logits.log_softmax(-1))).sum(-1) loss = (mask * per_example).mean() loss.backward() assert mask.tolist() == [True, False, False] torch.testing.assert_close(target[0], target.new_tensor([81/82, 1/82])) expected = (aug_logits.detach().softmax(-1) - target) * mask[:, None] / 3 torch.testing.assert_close(aug_logits.grad, expected) assert clean_logits.grad is None cross_entropy = -(target * aug_logits.detach().log_softmax(-1)).sum(-1) entropy = -(target * target.log()).sum(-1) torch.testing.assert_close(cross_entropy, entropy + per_example.detach()) print("accepted", mask.tolist(), "KL", loss.item(), "gradient", aug_logits.grad.tolist()) ``` ### How the text augmentation is constructed UDA uses English–French and French–English translation models to obtain paraphrases. It samples translations with a decoding temperature instead of always choosing the best beam. Generating the same paraphrase repeatedly adds little diversity; sampling too aggressively can change the meaning. The decoding temperature controlling this transformation is distinct from the target-softmax temperature $T$ above. The translation systems were trained on parallel data: “unlabelled” here means no target classification labels for each augmented review, not an absence of supervision anywhere in the pipeline. For topic classification, the paper also develops TF-IDF-based word replacement. Its original recipe selects word positions before WordPiece segmentation, rather than perturbing a subword embedding vector. Let $a_i$ be a word's TF-IDF score in the sentence, $C=\max_i a_i$, and $Z=\frac1n\sum_i(C-a_i)$. The replacement probability is $$ \pi_i=\min\left(\rho\frac{C-a_i}{Z},1\right). $$ Low-scoring positions are replaced more often. Replacement words are sampled with weights proportional to $S_{\max}-S(w)$, where $S(w)=\operatorname{freq}(w)\operatorname{IDF}(w)$ is computed over the corpus. The two distributions answer different questions: which position to change and which vocabulary word to insert. For sentence scores $(3,1,0)$ and $\rho=0.7$, $Z=5/3$ and the probabilities are $(0,0.84,1)$. Clipping changes the expected replacement count from $\rho n=2.1$ to $1.84$. With vocabulary scores $(30,10,0)$, the insertion distribution is $(0,0.4,0.6)$. These are constructed scores for checking the formulas, not scores of particular English words. ```python import numpy as np score = np.array([3., 1., 0.]) difference = score.max() - score probability = np.minimum(.7 * difference / difference.mean(), 1.) np.testing.assert_allclose(probability, [0., .84, 1.]) assert np.isclose(probability.sum(), 1.84) vocabulary_score = np.array([30., 10., 0.]) weight = vocabulary_score.max() - vocabulary_score np.testing.assert_allclose(weight / weight.sum(), [0., .4, .6]) print("position probabilities", probability, "expected changes", probability.sum()) ``` Equal TF-IDF scores give $Z=0$; equal vocabulary scores give a zero sampling normalizer. A production implementation needs a stated fallback for these cases. More generally, low TF-IDF does not imply that a word is irrelevant to the target: negation can reverse sentiment. Validate the augmentation on examples with known labels and inspect meaning-changing failures. Fluent output and a retained keyword do not prove invariance. ### Training Signal Annealing acts on labelled examples A small labelled set can be revisited many times while the much larger unlabelled pool is still being processed. UDA's Training Signal Annealing (TSA) suppresses the labelled loss for examples already predicted confidently **in their correct class**. With $C$ classes and training progress $u=t/T_{\mathrm{steps}}$, its threshold is $$ \eta_t=\frac1C+\left(1-\frac1C\right)a(u). $$ The three schedules in the paper and code use $a(u)=u$, $a(u)=e^{5(u-1)}$ and $a(u)=1-e^{-5u}$. The exponential schedule releases most labelled examples late; the logarithmic schedule raises the ceiling earlier. The formulas approach the endpoints differently: the exponential threshold starts slightly above $1/C$, and the logarithmic threshold ends slightly below 1. The text implementation keeps an example when $p_\theta(y_i\mid x_i)\le\eta_t$ and normalizes over the **kept labelled examples**: $$ b_i=\mathbf1[p_\theta(y_i\mid x_i)\le\eta_t],\qquad \mathcal L_s= \frac{\sum_i b_i[-\log p_\theta(y_i\mid x_i)]} {\max(1,\sum_i b_i)}. $$ This is the opposite selection pressure from unlabelled confidence masking: TSA withholds already-easy human-labelled examples, whereas the unlabelled gate accepts only confident model-generated targets. The original implementation uses different denominators for the two terms. Changing both to an average over accepted examples changes the unlabelled regularizer's effective weight. For three classes and halfway through a linear schedule, the ceiling is $2/3$. Suppose the probabilities assigned to the human targets are $0.9$, $0.2$ and $0.5$. TSA retains the second and third examples, giving $(-\log0.2-\log0.5)/2\approx1.151293$. The second prediction can have maximum probability $0.7$ in a wrong class. Testing that maximum instead of the human-target probability would discard a confidently wrong example that needs labelled correction. ```python import math import torch import torch.nn.functional as F probability = torch.tensor([[.9, .06, .04], [.7, .2, .1], [.2, .3, .5]], dtype=torch.float64) labels = torch.tensor([0, 1, 2]) logits = probability.log().requires_grad_() ce = F.cross_entropy(logits, labels, reduction="none") threshold = 1/3 + (1 - 1/3) * .5 correct = logits.detach().softmax(-1)[torch.arange(3), labels] keep = correct <= threshold loss = (ce * keep).sum() / keep.sum().clamp_min(1) loss.backward() assert keep.tolist() == [False, True, True] assert abs(loss.item() - (-math.log(.2) - math.log(.5))/2) < 1e-12 assert (probability.max(-1).values <= threshold).tolist() == [False, False, True] torch.testing.assert_close(logits.grad[0], torch.zeros(3, dtype=logits.dtype)) # No retained labelled example gives zero loss and zero gradient. all_easy = torch.tensor([[.9, .1], [.95, .05]], dtype=torch.float64).log() all_easy.requires_grad_() gate = all_easy.detach().softmax(-1)[:, 0] <= .5 empty = (F.cross_entropy(all_easy, torch.zeros(2, dtype=torch.long), reduction="none") * gate).sum() / gate.sum().clamp_min(1) empty.backward() assert empty.item() == 0 and all_easy.grad.count_nonzero() == 0 print("TSA mask", keep.tolist(), "labelled loss", loss.item()) ``` The original [`get_tsa_threshold` and `create_model`](https://github.com/google-research/uda/blob/960684e363251772a5938451d4d2bc0f1da9e24b/text/uda.py) provide the exact gate, temperature and reduction semantics. The examples above execute these computations on specified arrays; they do not run a translation system or reproduce IMDb performance. The initialization also changes the result. The IMDb entries in [UDA, Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12848v6#S4.T4) are test-error percentages; both rows below use 20 labelled reviews and sequence length 512: | Initialization | Without UDA | With UDA | | --- | ---: | ---: | | BERT LARGE | 11.72 | 4.78 | | BERT LARGE additionally adapted on in-domain unlabelled text | 6.50 | 4.20 | Thus 4.20% includes both in-domain adaptation and UDA. The fully labelled BERT LARGE reference uses 25,000 labelled reviews and reports 4.51%. Comparing 4.20 with 4.51 mixes different supervision and initialization protocols; comparing 6.50 with 4.20 isolates the UDA addition within the paper's in-domain-adapted, 20-label setting. These published numbers are not results of the small programs here. FixMatch, developed next, uses a thresholded **hard** target from a weak view rather than UDA's soft distribution target.
